title: ghosts building walls
subtitle: Corridors of perception
intro:
In Chinese folklore, the phenomenon of guǐ dǎ qiáng (鬼打墙)—ghosts building walls—describes when someone lost at night, in fog or unfamiliar terrain, walks in what feels like a straight line and returns to where they started. No wall is seen or felt; there is only the fact of return. Two explanations exist. First, the folkloric, where the living bump into barriers constructed by the mischevious dead; second, the perceptual, positing that bodies deprived of external reference points will tend to veer off the normal and walk in circles.

Both record the invisible compulsion to recur. But circling is not always a failure of orientation; it may be closer to our default setting. Recurrence is what minds do once they have run out of data to process, and that tendency to spiral, to confabulate, to revisit and reconstitute the familiar, can be seen from our experience of dreams and hallucinations.

These rooms are built from walls. Though furnished with the ordinary cues of the gallery, you may find yourself disoriented and returning to the origin. As with the mischevious guǐ dǎ qiáng, that origin may not always be the same.
note:
Founded in Berkeley in the early 1990s around legendary art theorist Cornelius Grossburger, the collective works from an inherited discipline: a set of instructions, unnumbered and incomplete, but kept vital via the group's joint practice.

 The collective has no public face and does not share its dictates. Members cite Dadaism, Oulipo, and Wittgenstein as formative influences; while the connection may not be evident in the work itself, the resemblance is manifest in the puzzles and analogies to which the collective frequently recurs. Art, they remind us, is both a game to be played and a mystery to be solved.

From Berkeley, the collective has since spread internationally to New York, Paris, Hanoi, Vancouver, Luxembourg, São Paulo, Fez, and elsewhere. For this exhibition, members were invited to respond to the theme of guǐ dǎ qiáng (鬼打墙) and caption the results. Although they vary widely in style and tone, each contributor claims to remain faithful to Grossburger's original vision; another ghost, another wall, another origin returned to.
note1:
None of the work here is signed with real names. Its makers describe themselves, when pressed, as members of a collective without a public face, formed around what several call an inherited discipline: a set of instructions, numbered but incomplete, and laid down by a single legendary teacher around Berkeley in the early 90s.

Though uniformly reluctant to disclose their rules, the members variously describe themselves as inspired by Dadaism, Oulipo, the Frankfurt school, Wittgenstein, and Bach. Since the work of the collective bears no resemblance to any of the above, we cannot determine if these precursors are imagined, or real and governed by some abstract law of resemblance.

From Berkeley, the practitioners of the collective have spread to New York, Paris, Hanoi, Vancouver, Luxembourg, Sao Paulo, Fez, and elsewhere; it is a global diaspora. We asked each member to respond to the theme of guǐ dǎ qiáng. Despite differences of medium and intent, they all claim their contributions maintain fidelity to the discipline; another origin returned to.

works.title: Figure I
works.caption: Figure and ground: U+Σ².
works.description: In formidable and expressive brushstrokes, Watanabe depicts a towering figure. Or is it a cross draped with a sheet? Similarly, is “I” a number (a figure!) or the subject? “I wanted to pun on figuration, on the self, on the unreliability of perception,” said Watanabe. “I tried to blur the line between real and imagined. That is the ghost wall.”

works.title: Labyrinths
works.caption: The heart of the, labyrinth.
works.description: Haines' meticulously staged sculpture/photograph alludes to Jorge Luis Borges, the Argentinean writer whose stories take disorienting metaphysical turns. “I love Borges,” she told us. “He teaches us that reality is a kind of game, played according to rules of which we are ignorant. But we try to find out; reality as a detective novel!”

works.title: The Finite Torment of Purgatory
works.description: This marvelous depiction of purgatory, in ink and acrylic, shows a parade of phantoms clustered around the central, Dante-esque portal to other realms. Gupta adds: “It's purgatory and not hell because there's an escape. Or at least, we think there is; they might be ghost-walls leading to further torment.”
works.caption: A circlet of midnight fire.

works.title: Black Lodge
works.caption: Where to get a hundred damn fine cups of coffee?
works.description: In this pen-and-ink drawing of roiling spectral energy, Saint-Nugent takes us back to a key influence. “In the 90s, Twin Peaks appeared out of nowhere and started doing television very, very differently. I don't want to say too much, but I think of the Black Lodge [a location in the show] as the spiritual locus of Twin Peaks, a kind of home for the guǐ dǎ qiáng. The show is all about the walls.”

works.title: Le petit fantôme
works.caption: Remorsefully, scored.
works.description: Thibodeaux's little ghost, surrounded by a patchwork quilt of wall, has a quiet domestic energy, rather different from the sinister or ambiguous forces seen elsewhere in the exhibit. “Home is something we project, or if you will, hallucinate onto place. I wanted my ghost to capture some of that projected warmth, a positive spin on the guǐ dǎ qiáng.”

works.title: Disguise
works.caption: The top and bottom of a heap of clothes.
works.description: This enigmatic work presents a figure completely disguised by fabric, or perhaps, the empty disguise itself. In this case, the wall and the ghost are the same. According to Kruschenko, “The goal here was, paradoxically, to embody absence, in all its attendant ambiguity. Is anybody in there? You'll never know.”

works.title: Destination
works.caption: A pile of rubbish.
works.description: Tsyrlin makes meticulous 3D models and then post-processes the results to provide what he calls the “filmic gloss”. He added: “I imagine the movie then I select the moment. In this case, it's about a wanderer led by ghost walls to some sort of apocalyptic trash hole. I would watch that.”

works.title: The Tartar Steppe
works.caption: Gross municipal product.
works.description: Dino Buzzati's haunting novel is made manifest as architectural projection, part blueprint, part dreamscape. Fang said: “I read the book over the summer and sort of iterated my way into the existential madness of the Bastiani Fortress... I wanted it to feel like a state of mind. It's all about boundaries, implicitly, obsessively maintained... pure ghost-wall energy.”

works.title: Brainhead
works.caption: Two halves of the symbolic brain.
works.description: This disturbing linocut shows a brain emerging like a mushroom cloud from the skull of a Frankenstein-like being. “It's all about the brain, you know, perception, art, structure, and all that,” Willingdon told us, “I guess I wanted to draw attention to the organ instrumenting all that nonsense, without invoking ghosts.”

works.title: Flag
works.caption: redblack, red|black
works.description: With an aplomb reminiscent of Jasper Johns, Gross transforms the signal flag into something both universal and obscure, a sort of empty signifier. “I think of semiotics as characterized by walls, dividing what is meant from what is not meant. I identified the ghost wall with the challenge of a blank referent.”

works.title: View of Thornwood at Night
works.caption: Flower of Thornwood.
works.description: Whittaker literally inteprets the ghost wall as a fence, seen at night, with a distant town to offer perspective. The murk and striations in the foreground suggest that darkness is playing tricks on the viewer, or that elements of the fence are perceptually disarranged. “A fence would seem to anchor you, but you find it leads your eyes into the distance and makes what is close uncertain,” Whittaker offered.

works.title: Deliquescent Stair
works.caption: Farside of the coder.
works.description: Rivering's architectural practice is on impressive display with this elegant staircase—a guiding form—developed in the pallid, milky tones of the stereotypical ghost. Rivering offered: “I want to interpret the guǐ dǎ qiáng as a metaphor for the invisible guidance, the inevitability if you like, of good architecture. Circling, return, as ergonomics or natural use rather than haunting.”

works.title: Suspicious Cyanotype
works.caption: Drywall doesn't need nails.
works.description: Nothing here is what it seems; hence ‘suspicious’. “The joke is it's a painting, not a cyanotype,” Leung commented. Like Xu Bing's A Book from the Sky, Leung bookends her painting with meaningless ideograms, “ghost letters” as she calls them, “describing the ghost walls of the painting's spine”.

works.title: Rumours (after Bruegel)
works.caption: Endpoints of the bridge.
works.description: This piece evokes a typically human pastime: gossip, here visibly communicated amongst the huddled crowd. “Ghosts are social programs,” de Fleck stated. “They are artefacts of superstition, of outmoded conventions, of hearsay and religious fanaticism... My painting presents this aetiology explicitly. Humans themselves are the ghosts building walls.”
